steps.title: Start with the information bottleneck and show why a token needs a way to look outward
steps.topic: Establishes that attention lets each output position inspect every input position directly instead of relying on a single recurrent hidden state.

steps.title: Define the query vector as the representation of what one token is looking for
steps.topic: Defines a query vector for each token and explains that it expresses the information that token needs from the surrounding sequence.

steps.title: Trace one query as it compares with the sequence without confusing searching with contributing
steps.topic: Shows that a token's query is compared against every other token's key, while the corresponding value is reserved for the information eventually contributed.

steps.title: Connect the query-key comparison to an attention score and preview the computation that follows
steps.topic: Introduces the query's role in the dot-product score, including scaling by the key dimension, while leaving score normalization and value aggregation to the next sections.

teaches: Why attention needs a per-token representation of what that token is looking for
How a query vector participates in comparisons with keys
Why the query vector is distinct from the value vector
How the query-key dot product becomes an attention score
Why the score is scaled by the square root of the key dimension
assumes: Basic vector operations, including dot products
A sequence of tokens and token positions
The existence of key and value vectors, which are developed in adjacent sections
Softmax normalization and weighted value aggregation, which are developed in later chapters
plan.opening_promise: After this section, you will be able to identify a query vector, explain what information it represents for a token, and trace how it initiates that token's search across the sequence.
